questions.q: Define topic, partition, offset and replica, and the relationships between them.
questions.a: A **topic** is purely logical — a name; no file on disk is named after it. A **partition** is the real object: one append-only log on disk, and a topic is a set of them. An **offset** is a monotonically increasing integer scoped to one partition, so a record is uniquely identified by `(topic, partition, offset)` and there is no topic-wide offset. A **replica** is a copy of one partition on another broker; `replication.factor` applies per partition, with one leader serving all reads and writes and the followers fetching from it.

questions.q: Why can't the number of useful consumers in a group exceed the partition count?
questions.a: Within one group each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, so that assignment can never give a fifth consumer anything on a four-partition topic — it simply sits idle. Partition count is therefore the parallelism ceiling for a group, and it has to be chosen when the topic is created because raising it later is a one-way door that breaks key ordering.

questions.q: What is the message key for? What happens when it is null?
questions.a: The key selects the partition via `toPositive(murmur2(keyBytes)) % numPartitions`, so the same key always lands on the same partition — that is the only mechanism Kafka offers for ordering related records. With a null key the **sticky partitioner** takes over: it fills one partition until the batch is full or `linger.ms` expires and only then switches, which is batching behaviour and not per-record round-robin.

questions.q: What are the consequences of increasing the partition count on a live topic? Can you decrease it, and why not?
questions.a: Changing the partition count changes the divisor in the key hash, so roughly half the keys move to a different partition while their older records stay where they were — the consumer stops seeing a key's events in order across the cutover. You cannot decrease it: each partition is its own log with its own offset sequence, and merging two logs would mean inventing offsets that consumers have already committed against. The only order-preserving way to resize is a new topic plus a controlled migration.

questions.q: Read `Replicas: 2,3,1 · Isr: 2,3` — what does it tell you?
questions.a: Three replicas are configured but only two are in sync: broker 1 has fallen behind by more than `replica.lag.time.max.ms` and has been dropped from the ISR. Broker 2 is first in the replica list, so it is the preferred leader. The practical consequence is that with `min.insync.replicas=2` you are one failure away from producers being rejected, and `acks=all` now means only those two replicas — the redundancy you think you have is not the redundancy you have.

questions.q: Two groups read the same topic. Where is each group's progress kept, and how does Kafka keep them from interfering?
questions.a: Each group's committed offsets live in the internal compacted topic `__consumer_offsets`, keyed by `(group.id, topic, partition)`, so the groups never share a row and reading is non-destructive anyway. That is how one topic serves both shapes at once: consumers inside a group split partitions (queue), while separate groups each see the full stream (pub/sub). No exchange or copy is involved.

questions.q: A topic has 3 partitions and you need 30 consumers working in parallel while preserving order per user_id. How? Give the trade-offs of each option.
questions.a: **Repartition to 30+ via a new topic** — keyed by `user_id`, migrated deliberately; preserves ordering going forward but is a migration, and the old data's ordering across the cutover is lost. **Fan out inside the consumer** — one consumer per partition that dispatches to a worker pool keyed by `user_id`, so each key is handled by exactly one worker sequentially; keeps 3 partitions but you now own the in-process queueing, backpressure and offset-commit discipline (commit only up to the lowest unfinished record). **Share group** — removes the partition ceiling outright, but gives up ordering entirely, so it answers the parallelism half and fails the ordering half. **Two-stage pipeline** — consume 3 partitions and re-key into a wider internal topic; buys clean ordering at the cost of an extra hop, extra storage and at-least-once semantics between stages. The honest framing is that 3 partitions is the real constraint and only the first and fourth options actually remove it.

questions.q: At what scope does Kafka guarantee ordering? Name three ways to lose it even with the key set correctly.
questions.a: Ordering is guaranteed **within a partition only**, and only if the producer is configured correctly — never across partitions or topic-wide, because there is no shared clock and no global sequencer. Ways to lose it with a correct key: producer retries with `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection > 1` and idempotence off, so a later request lands ahead of one being retried; raising the partition count, which moves the key while its old records stay behind; and handing records to a thread pool after `poll()`, where Kafka delivered them in order and the application reordered them. A fourth: consuming through a share group, which trades ordering for parallelism.

questions.q: Why is Kafka fast despite writing to disk? Answer at the mechanism level.
questions.a: Appending to a log is sequential I/O, which on spinning disks and SSDs alike is an order of magnitude faster than random access — but that is only the first third of the answer. Writes go to the OS **page cache** rather than being fsynced per record, so the broker returns as soon as the data is in memory and durability comes from replication to other brokers instead of from flushing; a broker restart loses nothing because the page cache is the kernel's, not the process's. Reads of recent data are served from that same page cache, and Kafka sends them with **`sendfile`** so bytes go from page cache straight to the socket without being copied into user space or re-encoded — the broker never materialises the records at all. On top of that, records travel in **compressed batches** written to the log in the exact wire format the producer sent and the consumer expects, so the broker does no per-record work: no parsing, no re-framing, no per-message bookkeeping. The JVM heap stays small because the data lives in the kernel's cache, which also keeps GC pauses out of the path.
